To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the lack of costimulatory signals provided by tumor cells may explain why T cells do not respond to tumor antigens, that the addition of B7 to tumor cells can overcome this problem, that the immune system can be trained to respond to antigens it had previously ignored, and that the immune system may not be tolerant to tumor antigens.
the tumor-specific cytolytic T cells are unresponsive to tumor antigens due to lack of adequate costimulatory molecules, but can be activated upon provision of costimulatory signals.

1) CD28 costimulatory signals are essential for T-cell activation; 2) CD28 costimulation can be provided in vivo by transfecting tumor cells with B-7, and this enhances anti-tumor responses; 3) T-cell responses can be activated to tumor antigens that are otherwise silent; and 4) immunologic ignorance may contribute to the failure to respond to tumors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of costimulation in the generation of tumor immunity.
the mechanisms of immune responses to tumor-associated antigens and with the development of immunotherapeutic strategies based on the activation of T cells specific for such antigens.
understanding how the immune system can be manipulated to induce a vigorous anti-tumor immune responses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
tumor antigens are not necessarily "self" and that the immune system can respond to these antigens, but only when costimulation is provided.
tumor antigens are not ignored, and the T cells are not tolerant, but the T cells are ignorant.
costimulation and ignorance are two major mechanisms responsible for the lack of an effective anti-tumor immune reponse.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
tumor-specific CD8+ T cells are rendered tolerant to tumor antigen in the absence of B7-CD 28 costimulation, but are ignorant in its presence.
tumor cells are not professional antigen presenting cells, but can present tumor antigens in the context of MHC class I and II molecules, and thus may be able to induce an anti-tumor T-cell response.
tumor-specific CTL can be generated and that the tumor-specific CTL response can be amplified by B7 transfection of tumor cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
costimulation is required for the activation of CTL specific for many tumor antigens and that CTL specific for tumor antigens that are not costimulated may be in a state of ignorance.
tumor cells may express tumor-associated antigens that are recognized by cytolytic T cells but that these antigens are "invisible" because they are not associated with costimulatory molecules.
the immune system can respond against tumors expressing MHC class I and "foreign" antigens.
